blocks.content: 1. Introduction

Picture two pizza places in your neighborhood. The first one keeps a delivery rider on payroll around the clock. He clocks in at nine, sits in the back room, and waits. During dinner rush ten orders land at once and he cannot keep up. On a slow Tuesday afternoon zero orders come in and he still gets paid to sit there.

The second pizza place uses Swiggy or Zomato. Nobody is on payroll. The moment an order comes in, the app finds a nearby rider, that rider races over, picks up the food, delivers it, and the assignment ends. The restaurant pays only for that one delivery and nothing else.

Serverless architecture applies the second model to computing. Servers still exist somewhere, someone still owns racks of physical machines running your code, but you never see them, never patch them, and never decide how many to keep running. You hand the cloud provider a function, tell it what should trigger that function, and walk away. The provider runs exactly as much compute as your traffic needs and nothing more.

Serverless computing means you deploy individual functions instead of provisioning servers, and the cloud provider automatically handles provisioning, scaling and patching the machines your code runs on.

blocks.title: Why this matters for interviews
blocks.content: Interviewers bring up serverless whenever a workload sounds spiky or event driven: sending a confirmation email, resizing an image, reacting to a webhook. Explaining serverless correctly, including where it breaks down, signals that you see it as a tool for specific problems rather than a universal replacement for backend servers.
2. What Serverless Actually Means

The name is a bit of a lie. There is no computing without a server somewhere executing instructions. What actually disappears is your responsibility for that server. You stop choosing instance sizes, stop patching operating systems, stop deciding how many machines to run at three in the morning.
2.1 Servers still exist, you just do not manage them
blocks.text: 2.1 Servers still exist, you just do not manage them

blocks.content: Think about the difference between renting a car and using a taxi app. With a rented car you still own the responsibility of fueling it, parking it, and servicing it, even on days you never drive. With a taxi app a driver and car appear when you need a ride and disappear the moment the ride ends. You never think about the vehicle between rides.

Traditional servers, even virtual ones like an EC2 instance, work like the rented car. You provision a machine, and it runs continuously whether or not it is doing useful work, and you are billed for every hour it exists. A serverless function works like the taxi. The cloud provider keeps a pool of machines ready behind the scenes, and your code only occupies one of them for the duration of a single invocation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271708-445228501.png
blocks.alt: A traditional server running continuously and mostly idle, compared to a function that is invoked only when a request arrives

blocks.content: 2.2 What serverless does not mean

["It does not mean there are no servers. It means the provider owns the server management problem instead of you.","It does not mean everything is free. You still pay, just per invocation and per resource used instead of per hour of server uptime.","It does not mean you should replace every backend with functions. Plenty of workloads are still a better fit for a normal server or container.","It does not make statelessness or execution limits disappear. Those constraints are the price of the model, covered later in this lesson."]
items: It does not mean there are no servers. It means the provider owns the server management problem instead of you.
It does not mean everything is free. You still pay, just per invocation and per resource used instead of per hour of server uptime.
It does not mean you should replace every backend with functions. Plenty of workloads are still a better fit for a normal server or container.
It does not make statelessness or execution limits disappear. Those constraints are the price of the model, covered later in this lesson.

blocks.content: 3. The FaaS Model

The technical name for what most people mean by serverless is Function as a Service, or FaaS. Instead of deploying an application that runs continuously and listens for requests, you deploy a single function. The provider decides when to run it, on what hardware, and shuts it down the instant it finishes.
3.1 Function as a Service, the basic idea
blocks.text: 3.1 Function as a Service, the basic idea

blocks.content: A FaaS function is small and focused on purpose. It receives an event as input, does one job, returns a result, and exits. There is no long running process listening on a port. The provider is the one listening, and it invokes your function code only when something relevant happens.

Because each invocation is independent, the provider can run thousands of copies of the same function at the same time during a traffic spike, and zero copies when nobody is using it. You never provision that concurrency yourself.
3.2 The major providers
Every major cloud has its own FaaS product, and the concepts map almost one to one across them.

blocks.content: 4. Event-Driven Triggers
A function never runs on its own. Something has to trigger it. Serverless platforms are built around events, and the trigger you attach to a function determines what kind of workload it is good for.
4.1 The four common trigger types

{"headers":["Trigger type","What fires the function"],"rows":[["HTTP request","A client calls an API endpoint through an API gateway"],["File upload","A new object lands in a storage bucket"],["Queue message","A message arrives on a queue or topic"],["Schedule","A cron style rule fires at a fixed time or interval"]]}
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272994-630864665.png
blocks.alt: Four trigger types, an HTTP request, a file upload, a queue message and a schedule, all firing the same function

blocks.content: 4.2 How a function receives event data
blocks.text: 4.2 How a function receives event data

blocks.content: Whatever triggers the function, the provider packages the details of what happened into an event object and passes it as the first argument to your handler. An upload trigger hands you the bucket name and the key of the new file. A queue trigger hands you the message body. A schedule trigger hands you almost nothing beyond the time it fired, since a cron job usually does not need any input.

blocks.title: The event shape is provider specific
blocks.content: AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions and Azure Functions all format their event objects differently. Code that reads event.Records[0].s3 on AWS will not run unchanged on Azure. This is one of the reasons FaaS code tends to be tightly coupled to a single provider.
5. The Cost Model: Pay Per Invocation
blocks.text: 5. The Cost Model: Pay Per Invocation

blocks.content: A traditional server bills you for existence. An EC2 instance or a virtual machine costs money every hour it is running, whether it handled a million requests that hour or zero. A serverless function flips this completely: you are billed for the number of invocations and the compute time each invocation actually consumed, rounded to the nearest fraction of a second.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272995-988911858.png
blocks.alt: A traditional server billed at a flat rate for every hour it runs, compared to a serverless function billed only per invocation

blocks.content: 5.1 When this saves money, and when it does not
blocks.text: 5.1 When this saves money, and when it does not

blocks.content: If your traffic is spiky or unpredictable, serverless can be dramatically cheaper. A function that fires a hundred times a day costs almost nothing, while a server sitting there waiting for those hundred requests still costs a full day of uptime.

If your traffic is steady and high, the math flips. A server running at high utilization all day is usually cheaper per request than paying for the same volume of individual invocations. Serverless pricing is optimized for bursts and idle time, not for sustained heavy load.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["No servers to provision, patch or capacity plan","Cold starts add latency for functions that have not run recently"],["Scales automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent runs","A hard execution time limit forces long jobs to be redesigned"],["You pay only for the time your code is actually running","Local testing and debugging are harder than for a normal server"],["Great fit for spiky, unpredictable, event driven traffic","Steady, high volume traffic is often cheaper on dedicated servers"]]}
6. Cold Starts: The Practical Downside

This is the tradeoff that trips up almost everyone the first time they build on serverless. When a function has not run recently, the provider has to spin up a fresh execution environment before it can run your code: download your deployment package, start the language runtime, initialize any global variables. That startup tax is called a cold start, and it can add anywhere from tens of milliseconds to a few seconds of extra latency.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272995-229783464.png
blocks.alt: A request hitting an idle function that must boot a new instance before running, compared to a request hitting an already warm function that runs immediately

blocks.content: 6.1 Why cold starts happen

Providers do not keep every deployed function running all the time, that would defeat the entire pay-per-invocation model. Instead they keep a small pool of warm instances and spin new ones up on demand as traffic increases. The first request after a period of inactivity, or any request beyond what the warm pool can absorb, pays the cost of a fresh boot.

The runtime matters here. A Node.js or Python function typically cold starts in well under a second. A Java or dotnet function, with a heavier runtime to initialize, can take several seconds on a cold start.
6.2 Reducing cold start pain

Most providers offer provisioned concurrency, where you pay a small ongoing fee to keep a fixed number of instances permanently warm, trading away some of the pay-per-invocation savings for predictable latency. Keeping deployment packages small and dependencies light also shortens the boot time when a cold start is unavoidable.

blocks.title: Cold starts are a latency problem, not a correctness problem
blocks.content: A cold function still returns the right answer, it just takes longer to return it. For a background job that nobody is watching in real time, a cold start rarely matters. For a user facing API where every millisecond counts, it is usually the deciding factor against serverless.
7. Statelessness

A serverless function cannot assume anything it wrote to local disk or memory during one invocation will still be there the next time it runs. The provider is free to destroy that execution environment the moment your function returns, or reuse it for a completely unrelated request. There is no guarantee either way, so you have to code as if nothing survives.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272996-723646458.png
blocks.alt: A stateless function reading and writing to an external database and object storage instead of relying on its own local memory or disk between invocations

blocks.content: 7.1 Where state actually has to live
blocks.text: 7.1 Where state actually has to live

blocks.content: Anything a function needs to remember between calls has to live outside the function itself: a database for structured data, object storage for files, a cache like Redis for fast shared lookups. The function becomes a thin, disposable layer of logic that reads what it needs and writes what it produces, with all the durable state sitting in dedicated services built for exactly that job.

blocks.title: The /tmp directory is a trap
blocks.content: Most FaaS platforms give you a small scratch directory on local disk for temporary work during a single invocation. It is genuinely useful for things like unpacking a zip file mid execution, but it is not durable storage. It can vanish between invocations and it is never shared across concurrent copies of your function running at the same time.
8. Execution Time Limits

Every FaaS platform caps how long a single invocation is allowed to run. AWS Lambda cuts a function off at fifteen minutes no matter what it was doing. Google Cloud Functions and Azure Functions have their own caps in a similar range. Hit the limit and the platform kills the invocation, finished or not.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272996-222181532.png
blocks.alt: A task that starts running, hits the platform execution time limit, and gets forcibly killed before completing

blocks.content: 8.1 Why long running tasks are a bad fit
blocks.text: 8.1 Why long running tasks are a bad fit

blocks.content: The limit exists because the entire pricing and scaling model assumes short, bursty units of work. A function that ran for hours would tie up an execution slot the platform expects to reclaim quickly, and it would also rack up a bill that no longer looks like the cheap, on demand story serverless is sold on.

Video encoding, large scale data processing, machine learning training, and anything that needs a long lived connection such as a websocket server, all fight against this limit. They either time out mid job or have to be broken into smaller chunks that each fit inside the window.

blocks.title: The usual workaround is orchestration, not a bigger timeout
blocks.content: Long workflows are typically split into a chain of short functions coordinated by a state machine service like AWS Step Functions, with each step small enough to finish comfortably inside the time limit. If a task genuinely cannot be chunked, that is usually a sign it belongs on a regular server or a container instead.
9. Real World Usage Patterns
Serverless earns its keep on workloads that are short, triggered by an event, and do not need to hold state or a long connection open. A few patterns show up constantly in production systems.
9.1 Image thumbnail generation on upload

A user uploads a full resolution photo to object storage. That upload event fires a function that resizes the image into a few thumbnail sizes and writes them back to storage. The work is short, triggered by a single event, and does not need to run outside of that moment.
9.2 Webhook handlers and glue code

Payment providers, chat platforms, and third party APIs love to notify your system through webhooks: a small HTTP call fired the moment something happens on their end. A function is a natural fit here, since a webhook is exactly one event needing exactly one quick reaction, often just forwarding data from one managed service to another.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272997-812588134.png
blocks.alt: A function sitting between a payment service and a notification service, reacting to one event and forwarding it to the other

blocks.content: 9.3 Scheduled cleanup jobs

Plenty of housekeeping work only needs to run once an hour or once a day: deleting expired sessions, rotating logs, sending a daily summary email. A scheduled trigger firing a function is far simpler than keeping a dedicated server alive purely to run a task for a few seconds a day.
10. Worked Example: Image Upload to Thumbnail Pipeline
blocks.text: 10. Worked Example: Image Upload to Thumbnail Pipeline

blocks.content: Put the pieces together with a concrete pipeline you will see in real systems and in interviews. A user uploads a profile picture. Somewhere downstream, thumbnails need to exist for the app to render fast, small previews instead of full resolution images everywhere.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272998-472602911.png
blocks.alt: A user uploading an image to a storage bucket, which fires a thumbnail function that writes a resized image back to the bucket

blocks.content: 10.1 The event flow step by step
blocks.text: 10.1 The event flow step by step

blocks.content: ["The client uploads the original image directly to an object storage bucket, into a folder such as uploads.","The storage service emits an object created event the moment the upload finishes.","That event triggers a Lambda function, passing along the bucket name and the key of the new object.","The function downloads the original bytes, resizes them into one or more thumbnail dimensions, and uploads the results into a thumbnails folder in the same bucket.","The application reads thumbnail URLs straight from storage whenever it needs to render a preview."]
items: The client uploads the original image directly to an object storage bucket, into a folder such as uploads.
The storage service emits an object created event the moment the upload finishes.
That event triggers a Lambda function, passing along the bucket name and the key of the new object.
The function downloads the original bytes, resizes them into one or more thumbnail dimensions, and uploads the results into a thumbnails folder in the same bucket.
The application reads thumbnail URLs straight from storage whenever it needs to render a preview.

blocks.content: 10.2 Implementation: the Lambda handler
Here is a realistic handler for the thumbnail step, written for AWS Lambda using the SDK v3 and the sharp image library.

blocks.title: Watch your deployment package size
blocks.content: Native dependencies like sharp compile platform specific binaries. Bundling them incorrectly is one of the most common reasons a Lambda function works locally and fails in the cloud. Most teams package this kind of dependency as a Lambda layer instead of bundling it directly with the function code.
11. Serverless vs Traditional Servers
None of this makes serverless universally better or worse than running your own servers. It is a different set of tradeoffs, and the right choice depends entirely on the shape of the workload.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272998-847284965.png
blocks.alt: Spiky, unpredictable traffic pointing toward serverless, and steady, constantly high traffic pointing toward traditional servers

blocks.content: 11.1 Good fits vs bad fits

A rough rule of thumb: if the work is short, triggered by a clear event, and traffic is unpredictable, lean serverless. If the work is long running, needs a persistent connection, or runs at sustained high volume around the clock, lean toward regular servers or containers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396272998-155294005.png
blocks.alt: Thumbnail generation and webhook handling shown as good fits for serverless, video encoding and a persistent websocket server shown as bad fits

blocks.content: 11.2 The interview angle

When a system design interview drifts toward something spiky and event driven, like resizing uploaded images or reacting to a payment webhook, naming serverless and explaining why is a strong answer. The trap is treating it as the answer to every question. A high throughput API serving millions of steady requests a day, or a service that needs to hold a websocket connection open, is not a good serverless candidate, and saying so out loud is exactly what a strong candidate does.

blocks.title: The strongest answer names the tradeoff, not just the tool
blocks.content: Do not just say serverless. Say why: the workload is bursty, the cost of idle capacity would be wasted, and the function is short enough to fit comfortably inside the execution time limit. That reasoning is what interviewers are actually listening for.
